I have not run these examples on a live tenant: the payload and query are templates to adapt, and I flag what I could not verify. proposed.description: Getting a transcript is only the first handoff in a caption editor. After that, the words have to survive several clocks, a live preview, a style system, and a video encoder. I’m building Karaoke Captions , a React and TypeScript editor that transcribes and renders video locally. In an earlier post I gave an overview of the product. This time I want to walk through the implementation choices that make a word-by-word caption become a finished MP4. The interesting parts are the boundaries: compressed media to PCM, model output to editable timing, preview time to export time, and decoded frames to an MP4 container. The pipeline I keep separate from the interface The local workflow has six main stages: File / Blob → decode audio to 16 kHz mono Float32 PCM → transcribe in a Web Worker → normalise word timestamps and build phrases → edit text, timing and style → draw captions over decoded video frames → encode and mux the finished MP4 React owns the editing interface. The document holds the words and style choices. The transcription worker handles model work. The rendering code decides what a caption looks like at a given time. That separation lets me revise a font or a sentence without running speech recognition again. It also gives the preview and export a shared description of the video they’re supposed to produce. 1. GitHub Copilot runs $19/month per developer. Cursor Pro costs $20/month. Tabnine Enterprise lands at $15/seat. Add a code review tool, a testing assistant, and a documentation generator — you're at $80–120/month per engineer before you've written a line of code. Most teams pay that. Few measure ROI. Here's what nobody tells you: the tools that cost the most are rarely the ones delivering the most value. proposed.description: The Register writes that "The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds." In his weekly kernel update post, Torvalds said Linux 7.4 rc2 was a big release partly because it contained code he'd left out of rc1 because he'd been busy and it was already the largest such release in kernel history. But Torvalds said the other reason rc2 was big was "various AI fixes." Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September — its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That's many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds' post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. "This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true," he wrote. That's a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kerne
proposed.title: Linus Torvalds Wonders If Linux's AI-Prompted Patch Flood Has Peaked
